title.analysis: The title uses a counterintuitive outcome—score decline despite on-time payment—to challenge the report-card mental model. It accurately signals the script's central point that payment history is only one input and that reported balances, limits, inquiries, account status, model choice and file errors can change a score. 'Drops' is not a guaranteed consequence of paying on time: the score can rise, fall or remain unchanged depending on the model and entire file. The script eventually says this, but its opening 22-point story makes a specific outcome feel more deterministic than the evidence permits. At 0.49765x against ten frozen same-channel age peers and 0.47287x against five, the result is WEAK in both cohorts; public metadata cannot establish whether the topic, phrasing or distribution caused that result.
title.search_demand: Durable consumer-help intent around unexplained credit-score changes, utilization reporting, closing cards, inquiries, paid-off loans and mortgage preparation. Historical query volume and traffic-source data are unavailable.
title.script_alignment: Strong topical alignment: the hook shows a paid-in-full card with a higher reported balance, the body covers multiple score inputs, and the close gives a five-step checklist. The title is narrower than the script, which also critiques model fragmentation, dispute handling and lender incentives.

thumbnail.analysis: The registered maxresdefault JPEG was fetched once, preserved and inspected at 1280x720 and proportional 320x180. A worried cartoon man in a blue hoodie looks at a phone labeled 'CREDIT SCORE' with a large red downward arrow. Oversized black text reads 'STILL DROPS?!' and a thick curved arrow points back toward the phone. The three-word phrase, phone label and score-down symbol remain legible at mobile size. The image efficiently visualizes the title's paradox but does not show the crucial timing condition: a score changes from the credit-file snapshot and model, not because on-time payment itself is penalized. Historical upload art, CTR, A/B tests and causal performance contribution are unavailable.

script.analysis: The script has a clear household mystery, a recurring Thomas character and a useful organizing correction: a credit score is a model output from the file at a point in time, not a moral grade for paying bills. It moves from utilization timing through limits, inquiries, closure, credit mix, authorized users, model variation and errors, then pays off the mortgage setup and gives a practical checklist. The strongest advice is to inspect all reports, distinguish statement-close timing from the due date, avoid unnecessary applications and ask which model a lender uses. The main weakness is false precision. Universal utilization cliffs, point-loss ranges, removal timelines and model/population claims are presented as fixed even though FICO says the impact of one change depends on the complete file. Thomas is an unsourced composite, and the script stacks several separate hypothetical score movements into one causal story. The adversarial bureau-incentive section moves from documented dispute failures to an unsupported claim that opacity structurally benefits the system. The paper-only dispute and authorized-user 'clean history stays' advice are also too categorical.
claim_audit: SUPPORTED: CFPB guidance reviewed in January 2024 says paying a card on time can help scores but a high balance present when the score is calculated can still affect the result even if paid in full the next day. This supports the reported-balance timing mechanism, not the exact 22-point Thomas outcome.

SUPPORTED_WITH_CAVEAT: FICO's published factor categories are 35% payment history, 30% amounts owed, 15% history length, 10% new credit and 10% credit mix for the general FICO framework. FICO also says the percentages are broad population-level importance and a single factor's exact impact cannot be isolated without the full report. Calling 30% utilization a universal cliff and assigning 50-to-100-point losses is unsupported.

SUPPORTED_WITH_CAVEAT: FICO says a lender limit decrease or closure may raise utilization; the resulting score may fall, rise or stay the same because the entire file matters. Closed accounts can remain for years and continue helping history length. The script's utilization arithmetic is correct, but a fixed score response is not established.

SUPPORTED_WITH_CAVEAT: CFPB distinguishes hard inquiries after credit applications from soft inquiries such as prescreening and self-review. Hard inquiries can affect scores because models consider recency and frequency. FICO also groups qualifying mortgage, auto and student-loan rate-shopping inquiries by model-specific windows. The video's four-inquiry pattern, six-inquiry bankruptcy multiplier and 2.8-billion-mailer figure were not independently verified here.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: FICO says paying off a car loan can affect credit mix. It does not support a universal 10-to-25-point decline or the claim that a mortgage six weeks later necessarily costs a better rate. The effect is file- and model-dependent.

MISLEADING: The script says an authorized user's late mark remains for seven years after removal while the clean history stays. Reporting and removal practices vary; removing an authorized user commonly removes the account tradeline rather than selectively preserving only its positive history. No primary source reviewed supports the categorical 30-to-60-day or clean-history-stays claims.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: FICO documents multiple base and industry-specific score versions, including auto scores with a 250-to-900 range, and scores can differ by bureau and model. At the 2026-04-08 publication date, FHFA's 2022 approval of FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 existed, but the 2026-04-22 implementation announcement had not yet occurred. The transcript's universal statement that mortgage lenders currently use only FICO 2/4/5 and its exact 14- and 38-point model gaps were not fully verified.

OVERSTATED: The FTC's 1,001-participant study found one in four identified possible errors that might affect scores, one in five had a report modified after dispute, and about 5% had errors that could affect credit terms. Extrapolating the one-in-four figure into roughly 40 million Americans with meaningful errors 'right now' changes the study measure and ignores its 2012-era snapshot.

SUPPORTED_AS_ALLEGATION_OR_ORDER: CFPB sued Experian on 2025-01-07 alleging sham investigations and failure to convey relevant dispute information. CFPB ordered Equifax to pay a $15 million penalty on 2025-01-17 for improper investigations. These actions predate publication; allegations against Experian are not a final adjudication of every script claim.

UNSUPPORTED: The transcript's claim that credit bureaus and lenders profit from consumer confusion is an interpretation. Bureau data sales and risk-based pricing are real, but the reviewed sources do not establish a coordinated or structural causal incentive to keep scoring rules opaque.

CALCULATION_MISMATCH: For a $380,000 fully amortizing 30-year loan, monthly principal-and-interest payments are about $2,553.72 at 7.1% and $2,452.06 at 6.7%; the difference over 360 payments is about $36,599, not $31,200. Taxes, insurance, fees, points, prepayment and lender-specific pricing are omitted, so neither number is a universal borrower outcome.

PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED: CFPB says consumers can review reports without affecting scores and, since the pandemic, the nationwide reporting companies provide weekly access on request. The script's advice to use AnnualCreditReport.com is directionally sound. The assertion that a paper dispute creates legal standing that an online dispute does not is unsupported and should not be presented as legal advice.

topic.analysis: Durable consumer-credit education centered on why a score can change despite an unbroken on-time-payment record. The mechanisms are reported-balance timing, utilization, credit-limit changes, hard inquiries, account closure, credit mix, authorized-user reporting, score-model variation and file errors. The practical audience problem is preparing for credit applications without confusing a consumer score with the lender's model or a payment due date with a reporting snapshot. The strongest reusable angle is a dated worked example showing statement close, bureau reporting, payment due date and application date on one timeline. Avoid deterministic point promises and anti-bureau motive claims.
topic.audience_problem: Consumers may pay every bill on time yet misunderstand why the score available to them differs or changes before an important credit application.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Build a reporting-calendar explainer with one card statement and one mortgage application. Separate observed file changes from possible score responses, compare consumer versus lender scores, and include a correction path for actual report errors. This is more defensible than promising exact points from generic actions.

original_content_lesson.test: Test a source-led 'Statement Date vs Due Date' package against the broad score-drop package. Show a one-card reporting calendar in the first minute, identify the exact score model/population for every claim, and avoid promised point changes. Measure owned CTR, first-calendar retention and report-checklist conversion.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH for transcript coverage, image inspection, calculations, date order and cohort reproduction; MEDIUM for topic/package interpretation; LOW for causal performance explanation.
